questions.stem: In genetics, what is a mutation?
options: The process of copying a gene's DNA sequence into a molecule of messenger RNA
A permanent change in a gene's base sequence or in chromosome structure or number
A temporary change in the way a gene is expressed in response to the environment
The normal exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes in meiosis
questions.explanation: A mutation is a lasting change in genetic material, either in the base sequence of a gene or in chromosome structure or number. Crossing over during meiosis reshuffles existing alleles rather than creating new ones.

questions.stem: Which list contains only mutagens?
options: Ultraviolet light, insulin and vitamin D in the diet
Visible light, sound waves and chemicals in tobacco smoke
X-rays, enzymes in saliva and the warmth of the body
Ultraviolet light, X-rays and chemicals in tobacco smoke
questions.explanation: Mutagens are agents that increase the rate of mutation. UV light, ionising radiation such as X-rays, and many chemicals in tobacco smoke damage DNA. Visible light and sound waves do not.

questions.stem: DNA polymerase occasionally inserts the wrong base when DNA is copied. When is this kind of error most likely to produce a mutation?
options: During DNA replication, if the error is not repaired
During transcription, when mRNA is made from the DNA template strand
During translation, when amino acids are joined together at the ribosome
During digestion, when DNA in food is broken down into nucleotides
questions.explanation: Mutations arise when DNA is copied incorrectly and the error escapes the cell's repair systems, so it is passed to daughter cells. Errors in mRNA or protein are not copied into the DNA and do not count as mutations.

questions.stem: How does ultraviolet radiation from sunlight cause mutations in skin cells?
options: It stops all cell division in the skin, so no DNA can be copied
It adds extra chromosomes to skin cells during each cell division
It causes abnormal bonds between neighbouring DNA bases
It breaks down the cell membrane so that DNA leaks out of the cell
questions.explanation: UV light can cause adjacent bases on the same DNA strand, such as two thymines, to bond together. If not repaired, this distorts the DNA and can lead to copying errors, which is why sun exposure increases the risk of skin cancer.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a somatic mutation and a germline mutation?
options: A germline mutation occurs in gamete-forming cells, so it can be inherited
A somatic mutation occurs in cells that form gametes, so it can be inherited
A germline mutation affects only the person in whom it occurs
A somatic mutation is always harmful, while a germline one is neutral
questions.explanation: Germline mutations arise in cells that give rise to sperm or eggs and can be passed to offspring. Somatic mutations occur in body cells, affecting only the individual, for example in many cancers.

questions.stem: A man worked for many years with a chemical mutagen and developed lung cancer caused by mutations in his lung cells. Are his children at higher risk of inheriting these mutations?
options: No, because mutations in lung cells are somatic and are not passed to gametes
Yes, because any mutation in the body is copied into every sperm cell produced
Yes, because the cancer cells travel to the testes and form new sperm cells
No, because mutations caused by chemicals are always repaired before birth
questions.explanation: Lung cells are somatic cells, so their mutations are not inherited. Only mutations in the germline can be passed on. The chemical could have caused separate mutations in his germline cells, but the lung mutations themselves are not transmitted.

questions.stem: Which type of gene mutation replaces one base in the DNA with a different base?
options: Deletion
Inversion
Substitution
Insertion
questions.explanation: In a substitution, one nucleotide is swapped for another, changing a single codon. Insertions and deletions add or remove bases, and inversions reverse a section of a chromosome.

questions.stem: Why does inserting a single base into the coding region of a gene usually have a large effect on the protein?
options: It doubles the length of the gene, so the protein is twice as long
It stops transcription, so no messenger RNA can be made at all
It shifts the reading frame, altering every later codon
It changes only one codon, so a single amino acid is replaced
questions.explanation: Codons are read in groups of three, so adding or removing one base shifts the reading frame. All codons after the change are altered, which usually produces a non-functional protein, often with an early stop codon.

questions.stem: A substitution changes the codon GAA to GAG. Both codons code for the amino acid glutamic acid. What type of mutation is this?
options: A frameshift mutation, because the reading frame has shifted
A silent mutation, because the amino acid sequence is unchanged
A missense mutation, because a different amino acid is produced
A nonsense mutation, because a stop codon has been created
questions.explanation: The genetic code is degenerate, so more than one codon can code for the same amino acid. A substitution that does not change the amino acid is silent and usually has no effect on the phenotype.

questions.stem: In a gene of 300 codons, a mutation turns codon 5 into a stop codon. What does translation of this gene now most likely give?
options: A longer protein is made, because translation continues
A short, usually non-functional protein is made
A full-length protein with one different amino acid is made
A normal protein is made, because stop codons are ignored
questions.explanation: A substitution that creates an early stop codon is a nonsense mutation. Translation stops at that point, so the protein is shortened and usually cannot function. One different amino acid in a full-length protein describes a missense mutation.

questions.stem: The most common cystic fibrosis allele results from the deletion of three bases from the gene. Why does this not cause a frameshift?
options: The three deleted bases were in a stop codon, so the protein is simply longer
The cell inserts three new bases elsewhere, so the total length is restored
Three bases make one codon, so later codons are still read correctly
Deletions never cause frameshifts; only insertions of bases change the reading frame
questions.explanation: Removing exactly three bases removes one codon, so one amino acid is missing but the codons that follow are read normally. The protein is still faulty because of the missing amino acid. Deleting one or two bases would shift the frame.

questions.stem: In sickle-cell anaemia, a single base substitution in the beta-globin gene changes one amino acid in the haemoglobin protein. Which type of mutation is this?
options: Silent
Frameshift
Missense
Nonsense
questions.explanation: Changing one amino acid for another is a missense mutation. Here glutamic acid is replaced by valine, which alters haemoglobin so that red blood cells can become sickle-shaped when oxygen is low.

questions.stem: What is non-disjunction?
options: The reversal of a segment of a chromosome so that its genes run backwards
The exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes in meiosis
Chromosomes or chromatids failing to separate properly in cell division
The joining of two broken chromosome pieces in the wrong order after damage
questions.explanation: In non-disjunction, a pair of chromosomes or sister chromatids fails to separate, so some gametes receive an extra chromosome and others lack one. Fertilisation then produces a zygote with an abnormal chromosome number.

questions.stem: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by trisomy 21. What does this mean?
options: The person's chromosome 21 has a segment repeated three times
The person has 21 pairs of chromosomes instead of 23 pairs
The person's cells contain three copies of chromosome 21
The person's cells contain only one copy of chromosome 21
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 means an extra copy of chromosome 21, giving 47 chromosomes in total. It usually results from non-disjunction during meiosis in one parent.

questions.stem: Which condition results from a person having only one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome (45,X)?
options: Klinefelter syndrome
Down syndrome
Cystic fibrosis
Turner syndrome
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome occurs in females with one X chromosome. Klinefelter syndrome occurs in males with an extra X chromosome (47,XXY). Cystic fibrosis is caused by a gene mutation, not a change in chromosome number.

questions.stem: A section of a chromosome breaks off and becomes attached to a different, non-homologous chromosome. What is this chromosome mutation called?
options: Inversion
Duplication
Non-disjunction
Translocation
questions.explanation: Translocation moves a segment to a non-homologous chromosome. In an inversion the segment is reattached to the same chromosome the other way round, and in a duplication a segment is repeated.

questions.stem: Which type of chromosome mutation leaves a segment of a chromosome present twice?
options: Duplication
Deletion
Inversion
Translocation
questions.explanation: In a duplication a segment of a chromosome is repeated, so the genes in it are present in extra copies. A deletion removes a segment, and an inversion reverses one.

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, with the sex chromosomes XXY. Which condition does this indicate?
options: Sickle-cell anaemia
Klinefelter syndrome
Turner syndrome
Down syndrome
questions.explanation: An extra X chromosome in a male (47,XXY) is Klinefelter syndrome, usually resulting from non-disjunction. Down syndrome involves an extra chromosome 21, not an extra sex chromosome.

questions.stem: In a chromosome with the gene order A-B-C-D-E-F, a mutation produces the order A-B-E-D-C-F. Which mutation has occurred?
options: Duplication
Translocation
Inversion
Deletion
questions.explanation: The segment C-D-E has been reversed to E-D-C while staying on the same chromosome, which is an inversion. No genes have been lost or gained, and none have moved to another chromosome.

questions.stem: The risk of having a child with Down syndrome increases with the mother's age. Which explanation is most consistent with what is known about how trisomy 21 arises?
options: Errors in chromosome separation in egg formation become likelier with age
Older mothers' body cells gain extra chromosomes and pass them to the fetus
Chromosome 21 is mutated by the placenta as the pregnancy goes on
Older mothers' eggs are more often fertilised by two sperm at once
questions.explanation: Most trisomy 21 arises from non-disjunction during meiosis in the mother, and the likelihood of chromosomes failing to separate correctly during egg formation rises with maternal age. Changes in the mother's body cells are not passed to the fetus.

questions.stem: Why are chromosome mutations often more harmful than a single base substitution?
options: They can alter the number or arrangement of many genes at once
They always occur in gametes, so every one of them is inherited
They change the genetic code, so codons code for new amino acids
They happen only in older people, whose cells cannot repair them
questions.explanation: A chromosome mutation can delete, duplicate or rearrange many genes, or add or remove a whole chromosome, which upsets the balance of many gene products. A single substitution affects at most one codon.

questions.stem: In a type of leukaemia, a translocation joins part of chromosome 9 to chromosome 22 in white blood cell precursors, creating a fused gene that drives uncontrolled cell division. Which statement about this mutation is correct?
options: It is non-disjunction, because the patient has gained a whole extra copy of chromosome 22
It is a somatic chromosome mutation, so it is not passed on to the patient's children
It is a germline gene mutation, so every one of the patient's children will inherit it
It is a frameshift mutation caused by the insertion of a single base into chromosome 9
questions.explanation: The translocation moves part of one chromosome onto a non-homologous one, so it is a chromosome mutation. It arises in blood-forming body cells, not in gametes, so it is somatic and not inherited.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly relates genotype and phenotype?
options: The genotype changes throughout life to match the phenotype that is needed
The phenotype results from the genotype interacting with the environment
The genotype results from the phenotype interacting with the environment
The phenotype is determined only by the genotype, never by the environment
questions.explanation: The genotype is the set of alleles an individual carries; the phenotype is the observable characteristics. Environmental factors such as diet, sunlight and disease influence how genes are expressed, so both contribute to the phenotype.

questions.stem: Human height shows continuous variation, with many intermediate values. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: It is controlled by many genes (polygenes), and diet also affects it
It is controlled by one gene with two alleles, one completely dominant over the other
It is controlled by a gene on the Y chromosome, so only males show variation in it
It is controlled entirely by diet, so genes play no part in differences in height
questions.explanation: Polygenic traits are influenced by many genes, each adding a small effect, which produces a range of phenotypes. Environmental factors such as nutrition shift where an individual falls within that range.

questions.stem: Identical twins have the same genotype, yet one is noticeably taller after being raised in a home with better nutrition. What does this show?
options: A mutation must have occurred in the taller twin's growth hormone gene
Height is controlled by a single gene that is switched on by good food
The twins cannot be identical, because their phenotypes are different
The environment influences how the genotype is expressed
questions.explanation: Because identical twins share the same alleles, differences between them are mainly due to environmental influences on gene expression. Nutrition affects how fully the genetic potential for height is reached.

questions.stem: In regions of high ultraviolet radiation, darker skin helps protect folate in the blood, while in regions of low ultraviolet radiation lighter skin allows more vitamin D to be made. What does this illustrate?
options: Skin colour is controlled by one gene with a single dominant allele for dark skin
Ultraviolet radiation causes skin cells to mutate until the best colour is reached
Phenotypes have no effect on survival because humans can change their environment
The same phenotype can be favoured in one environment and disadvantaged in another
questions.explanation: Different phenotypes are acted on differently by environmental factors. Where UV is intense, darker skin is advantageous; where it is weak, lighter skin is. This differing selection helps explain the geographic pattern of human skin colour.

questions.stem: A gene mutation stops a person's skin cells producing the pigment melanin. Why would this phenotype be a particular disadvantage in a sunny, high-UV environment?
options: Without melanin, UV light passes straight through the body to the organs
Unprotected skin is more easily damaged by UV, raising the risk of skin cancer
Without melanin, the skin cannot absorb any vitamin D from the person's diet
Without melanin, the body cannot produce enough sweat to cool itself down
questions.explanation: Melanin absorbs UV radiation and protects skin cells from DNA damage. Without it, UV causes more mutations in skin cells, so sunburn and skin cancer are more likely. The same phenotype would be less disadvantaged where UV is weak.

questions.stem: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inherited condition in which a person cannot break down the amino acid phenylalanine. If detected at birth and treated with a low-phenylalanine diet, symptoms are largely prevented. What does this show?
options: The person's genotype changes once phenylalanine is removed from food
The environment can change how a harmful genotype affects the phenotype
The diet repairs the mutated gene so that the person no longer carries it
PKU is not genetic, because a change in diet is able to prevent it
questions.explanation: The diet does not change the genotype, but it prevents phenylalanine building up, so the harmful phenotype does not develop. This shows that phenotype depends on both genotype and environment.

questions.stem: Meiosis and fertilisation produce enormous genetic variety, yet biologists say mutation is the ultimate source of variation. Why?
options: It is the only process that creates completely new alleles
It shuffles existing alleles into new combinations during meiosis
It moves alleles from one population into another population
It removes harmful alleles from a population over generations
questions.explanation: Crossing over, independent assortment and fertilisation create new combinations of existing alleles, and gene flow moves alleles between populations, but only mutation produces new alleles.

questions.stem: A new mutation arises in a human gene. Which prediction about its effect is most accurate?
options: All mutations are favourable, because they increase genetic variation
Mutations occur only when the environment changes and a new trait is needed
Most are neutral or harmful; a few are favourable in some environments
All mutations are harmful, because they disrupt the function of proteins
questions.explanation: A mutation's effect depends on where it occurs and on the environment. Many have no effect or are harmful, but some produce traits that improve survival and reproduction. Mutations occur randomly; they do not arise because they are needed.

questions.stem: Most adult mammals stop producing lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar. In some human populations with a long history of dairy farming, many adults keep producing it because of a particular mutation. What best explains why this allele became common there?
options: Adults who could digest milk had a nutritional advantage and left more offspring
Drinking milk caused the mutation to occur in the cells of people who drank it
The allele spread because dairy farming increased the mutation rate in those people
Adults who could digest milk passed on lactase enzyme to their children in milk
questions.explanation: The mutation arose by chance. Where fresh milk was available, adults carrying it gained extra nutrition, survived and reproduced more, so the allele became more frequent. Drinking milk did not cause the mutation.

questions.stem: A mutation in a gene called CCR5 removes part of a protein on the surface of white blood cells that some strains of HIV use to enter cells. People with two copies of this mutated allele are highly resistant to those strains. What does this example show?
options: Resistance to HIV must be caused by antibodies passed on through the mutated gene
A mutation that disrupts a protein can be favourable if a disease is present
A mutation is favourable only if it makes a protein work better than the original
Mutations arise in response to infection so that the body can resist the pathogen
questions.explanation: Whether a mutation is favourable depends on the environment. Loss of the normal CCR5 protein has little effect in most people, but where these HIV strains are present it gives resistance. The mutation existed before HIV; it did not arise because of it.

questions.stem: A new allele arises by mutation in one person. Which condition must be met for it to affect the gene pool of future generations?
options: It must occur in a somatic cell and spread to the person's other cells
It must produce a favourable phenotype the moment it first appears
It must be caused by a mutagen rather than a natural copying error
It must occur in the germline and be passed on through reproduction
questions.explanation: Only mutations in cells that form gametes can enter the next generation. Once passed on, an allele's frequency may then change by natural selection or by chance. Neutral alleles can persist, so being favourable is not required, and the cause of the mutation does not matter.

questions.stem: Two populations live in different environments. A mutation that gives a slightly thicker layer of insulating fat arises in both. In which population is it most likely to increase in frequency?
options: Neither, because mutations cannot change the frequency of alleles
The population in a cold climate, where it improves survival
The population in a hot climate, where it causes overheating
Both equally, because mutations always spread at the same rate
questions.explanation: A phenotype's value depends on the environment. In the cold, extra insulation may improve survival and reproduction, so the allele tends to increase. In the heat it may be a disadvantage, so it tends to decrease.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an error in cell division leading to a mutation?
options: Chemicals in tobacco smoke binding to DNA in lung cells and altering a base
X-rays breaking both strands of the DNA in a cell exposed during medical imaging
A chromosome pair failing to separate in meiosis, giving an extra chromosome
A gene being switched off by methylation, with no change to its base sequence
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction is an error in the separation of chromosomes during cell division. Methylation silences a gene without changing its sequence, so it is not a mutation, and the tobacco and X-ray examples are damage by mutagens.

questions.stem: A study compares the rate of skin cancer in outdoor workers who regularly use sunscreen with those who do not. Which hypothesis is best tested by this study?
options: UV radiation causes mutations only in people who already carry a skin cancer allele
Skin cancer is inherited, so sunscreen use will have no effect on how often it occurs
Less UV exposure lowers the rate of mutations that lead to skin cancer
Sunscreen changes the alleles that workers pass on to their children in their gametes
questions.explanation: Sunscreen reduces UV reaching skin cells, so the study tests whether less exposure to a mutagen reduces somatic mutations and cancer. Skin cancer from sun exposure arises from somatic mutations, so it does not involve the alleles passed to children.
